title: Oil Just Jumped $5 in a Single Day. An Exxon Executive Says Prices Could Hit $160.
excerpt: Brent crude surged past $95 after Iran threatened to block two of the world's most important shipping lanes. Exxon warned that global inventories are approaching unheard of lows.
body:
Oil prices surged more than 5 percent on Monday after Iran threatened to expand its naval blockade beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Bab El Mandeb strait, the chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea that controls access to the Suez Canal. It was the biggest single-day move in weeks, and it came with a warning from one of the world's largest oil companies that the market is running out of cushion.

What Happened

Brent crude futures jumped $4.80 to $95.92 a barrel by early afternoon in New York. West Texas Intermediate rose $5.46, or 6.2 percent, to $92.82. Both benchmarks had fallen sharply last month — Brent dropped 19 percent in May, its steepest monthly slide since March 2020 — on hopes that a US-Iran deal was imminent.

Those hopes evaporated over the weekend. The US struck Iranian radar sites and drone facilities near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they responded by targeting a US base in Kuwait. US Central Command confirmed it intercepted two Iranian ballistic missiles aimed at American troops.

Then came the escalation: Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that Tehran is halting indirect negotiations with Washington and making plans to "completely" block the Strait of Hormuz while taking action at the Bab El Mandeb. Esmaeil Qaani, head of Iran's Quds Force, delivered the threat personally.

The Inventory Crisis

The geopolitical risk comes on top of a structural problem. At the Bernstein Strategic Decisions Conference last Thursday, ExxonMobil Senior Vice President Neil Chapman warned that global oil inventories are approaching dangerously low levels.

"We're approaching unheard of inventory levels. I mean, really, really low levels," Chapman said. "You can debate whether that's going to hit those really low levels in two weeks or three weeks. But once you get to that point, then you'll see price shoot up."

Chapman suggested prices could reach $160 a barrel if the drawdown continues. Countries and companies have been burning through crude stockpiles and tapping strategic petroleum reserves since the war began in early March, but that buffer is disappearing fast.

The India Dimension

For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, every dollar increase in crude translates directly to the current account deficit, fuel prices, and inflation. The Strait of Hormuz, which handled one-fifth of global oil and LNG flows before the war, has been largely shut since late February. India has already pivoted to buying from Venezuela, Brazil, and Angola, but the alternatives are more expensive and logistically complex.

If Bab El Mandeb is also disrupted, it would affect oil shipments routed through the Red Sea and Suez Canal — the alternate path India has relied on since Hormuz closed. Ship-tracking firm Kpler confirmed just 10 vessel crossings of Hormuz over the weekend, lower than the previous week.

The Indian rupee, already under pressure at around ₹95 per dollar, faces further strain. The Reserve Bank of India has spent $47 billion from its forex reserves over three months defending the currency. The RBI's monetary policy committee meets this week, and while economists expect rates to hold, the oil spike will weigh on every calculation.

The Ceasefire That Isn't

Hours after the oil spike, Lebanon announced a partial ceasefire between Hezbollah and Israel — a limited de-escalation that could create space for renewed US-Iran talks. Trump confirmed the arrangement, saying Hezbollah pledged through intermediaries not to attack Israel. But Netanyahu said Israeli operations in southern Lebanon would continue.

Trump dismissed the suspension of Iran talks in a CNBC interview, saying he "didn't care" if they were over. Prices trimmed some gains after his comments, but the market remains on edge.

"The longer the conflict continues, the lower commercial inventories will get," said Andrew Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates. "At which time prices spike. We are only a month or two away from that."

Sources: Reuters, WSJ, New York Post, AP, Kpler ship-tracking data
author: Diaspora Desk
